title: Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 11 — Signing Pleadings, Motions, and Other Papers; Representations to the Court; Sanctions (rule text with Advisory Committee Notes)
pub: Legal Information Institute, Cornell Law School
author: Advisory Committee on Civil Rules

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: Rule 11 supplies a relevant baseline for verifying legal and factual support in court filings and assigning responsibility to attorneys, firms and parties. However, it does not address AI capability, selective deployment, human–AI work allocation or operating-model redesign, so its position on the cluster’s principal proposition cannot be determined.
qs: (1) In General.* If, after notice and a reasonable opportunity to respond, the court determines that Rule 11(b) has been violated, the court may impose an appropriate sanction on any attorney, law firm, or party that violated the rule or is responsible for the violation.

st.t: Filing duties: AI use never displaces inquiry
st.an: Rule 11 directly supports the cluster’s central proposition: presenting or later advocating a filing certifies an inquiry reasonable under the circumstances, and the filing must be read before submission. Although the source does not address AI specifically, its tool-neutral duties, continuing responsibility, and bounded sanctions framework apply to AI-assisted filings.
qs: The obligations imposed under subdivision (b) obviously require that a pleading, written motion, or other paper be read before it is filed or submitted to the court.

kp.k: Court submissions certify reasonable legal and factual inquiry
kp.d: Rule 11(b) makes presenting a paper—including signing, filing, submitting, or later advocating it—a certification by an attorney or unrepresented party following inquiry reasonable under the circumstances. The certification covers improper purposes, legal justification, factual support, and justified denials. The document establishes legal obligations rather than discussing AI or measuring its effects.
qs: By presenting to the court a pleading, written motion, or other paper—whether by signing, filing, submitting, or later advocating it—an attorney or unrepresented party certifies that to the best of the person's knowledge, information, and belief, formed after an inquiry reasonable under the circumstances:
the claims, defenses, and other legal contentions are warranted by existing law or by a nonfrivolous argument for extending, modifying, or reversing existing law or for establishing new law;
the factual contentions have evidentiary support or, if specifically so identified, will likely have evidentiary support after a reasonable opportunity for further investigation or discovery;

kp.k: Reasonableness exceeds good faith but rejects hindsight
kp.d: The 1983 Notes describe a prefiling duty to investigate facts and law that is more stringent than the original good-faith standard. They direct courts to assess what was reasonable when the paper was submitted, considering available investigation time, reliance on clients or other lawyers, and the plausibility of the legal position, without chilling creative advocacy.
qs: The new language stresses the need for some prefiling inquiry into both the facts and the law to satisfy the affirmative duty imposed by the rule.
This standard is more stringent than the original good-faith formula and thus it is expected that a greater range of circumstances will trigger its violation.

The court is expected to avoid using the wisdom of hindsight and should test the signer's conduct by inquiring what was reasonable to believe at the time the pleading, motion, or other paper was submitted.

kp.k: Responsibility to the court cannot be delegated
kp.d: The 1993 Notes expressly describe the presenting person's responsibility as nondelegable. Rule 11(c)(1) permits sanctions against responsible attorneys, firms, or parties and requires joint law-firm responsibility for violations by partners, associates, or employees absent exceptional circumstances. The Notes also allow inquiry into the responsibility of co-counsel, other firms, and institutional parties.
qs: The person signing, filing, submitting, or advocating a document has a nondelegable responsibility to the court, and in most situations is the person to be sanctioned for a violation.
Absent exceptional circumstances, a law firm must be held jointly responsible for a violation committed by its partner, associate, or employee.
The revision permits the court to consider whether other attorneys in the firm, co-counsel, other law firms, or the party itself should be held accountable for their part in causing a violation.

kp.k: Later advocacy renews responsibility for written contentions
kp.d: The 1993 Notes distinguish new oral assertions, which Rule 11 does not cover, from later advocacy of positions already contained in court papers. Litigants may face sanctions for reaffirming contentions after learning they lack merit. The Notes also clarify that removing an express certification of reading did not remove the obligation to read papers before submission.
qs: The obligations imposed under subdivision (b) obviously require that a pleading, written motion, or other paper be read before it is filed or submitted to the court.

It does not cover matters arising for the first time during oral presentations to the court, when counsel may make statements that would not have been made if there had been more time for study and reflection.

However, a litigant's obligations with respect to the contents of these papers are not measured solely as of the time they are filed with or submitted to the court, but include reaffirming to the court and advocating positions contained in those pleadings and motions after learning that they cease to have any merit.

kp.k: Factual uncertainty is permitted within investigative limits
kp.d: Specifically identified factual contentions may await evidentiary support from further investigation or discovery, but this does not excuse an initial reasonable investigation. The 1993 Notes distinguish evidentiary support from ultimate success and require litigants not to persist in unsupported contentions or unwarranted denials. Formal amendment is not necessarily required; continued advocacy is the central concern.
qs: Tolerance of factual contentions in initial pleadings by plaintiffs or defendants when specifically identified as made on information and belief does not relieve litigants from the obligation to conduct an appropriate investigation into the facts that is reasonable under the circumstances; it is not a license to join parties, make claims, or present defenses without any factual basis or justification.
Moreover, if evidentiary support is not obtained after a reasonable opportunity for further investigation or discovery, the party has a duty under the rule not to persist with that contention.
That summary judgment is rendered against a party does not necessarily mean, for purposes of this certification, that it had no evidentiary support for its position.

kp.k: Legal innovation remains permissible under an objective standard
kp.d: The 1993 Notes protect nonfrivolous arguments for changing or creating law while rejecting sincere belief as a sufficient justification for patently frivolous arguments. Research, minority opinions, law-review support, and consultation with other lawyers are relevant considerations; expressly identifying an argument as seeking legal change warrants greater tolerance.
qs: This establishes an objective standard, intended to eliminate any “empty-head pure-heart” justification for patently frivolous arguments.

However, the extent to which a litigant has researched the issues and found some support for its theories even in minority opinions, in law review articles, or through consultation with other attorneys should certainly be taken into account in determining whether paragraph (2) has been violated.
Although arguments for a change of law are not required to be specifically so identified, a contention that is so identified should be viewed with greater tolerance under the rule.

kp.k: Sanctions prioritize deterrence rather than compensation
kp.d: The reproduced rule permits, rather than automatically requires, sanctions following a violation and limits their severity to sufficient deterrence. Available responses include nonmonetary directives, court penalties, and qualifying motion-based awards of directly resulting fees and expenses. The 1993 Notes identify educational programs and disciplinary referrals among possible responses and list culpability, repetition, litigation effects, and financial resources as relevant considerations.
qs: A sanction imposed under this rule must be limited to what suffices to deter repetition of the conduct or comparable conduct by others similarly situated.
Since the purpose of Rule 11 sanctions is to deter rather than to compensate, the rule provides that, if a monetary sanction is imposed, it should ordinarily be paid into court as a penalty.

The court has significant discretion in determining what sanctions, if any, should be imposed for a violation, subject to the principle that the sanctions should not be more severe than reasonably necessary to deter repetition of the conduct by the offending person or comparable conduct by similarly situated persons.

kp.k: Safe harbor encourages correction before motion-based sanctions
kp.d: Rule 11(c)(2) requires a separate sanctions motion specifying the challenged conduct and bars filing or presentation if that conduct is withdrawn or appropriately corrected within 21 days after service, or another court-set period. The 1993 Notes explain that service of the motion—not informal warning—starts the safe harbor and that timely withdrawal protects against the other party's sanctions motion.
qs: The motion must be served under [Rule 5](/rules/frcp/rule_5), but it must not be filed or be presented to the court if the challenged paper, claim, defense, contention, or denial is withdrawn or appropriately corrected within 21 days after service or within another time the court sets.

To stress the seriousness of a motion for sanctions and to define precisely the conduct claimed to violate the rule, the revision provides that the “safe harbor” period begins to run only upon service of the motion.

kp.k: Court-initiated sanctions have distinct safeguards and limits
kp.d: Sanctions require notice and a reasonable opportunity to respond, and an imposing order must explain the conduct and basis. Courts may initiate proceedings through a show-cause order; the Notes distinguish this route from motion-based safe harbor. Monetary sanctions cannot target represented parties for Rule 11(b)(2) legal-contention violations, and court-initiated monetary sanctions require a show-cause order before the relevant voluntary dismissal or settlement.
qs: An order imposing a sanction must describe the sanctioned conduct and explain the basis for the sanction.

Sanctions that involve monetary awards (such as a fine or an award of attorney's fees) may not be imposed on a represented party for causing a violation of subdivision (b)(2), involving frivolous contentions of law.

Since show cause orders will ordinarily be issued only in situations that are akin to a contempt of court, the rule does not provide a “safe harbor” to a litigant for withdrawing a claim, defense, etc., after a show cause order has been issued on the court's own initiative.

kp.k: Sanctions motions must not become litigation abuse
kp.d: The 1993 Notes discourage sanctions threats for minor violations and prohibit using such motions as substitutes for discovery or merits challenges. They warn against intimidation, unjust settlement pressure, cost escalation, and intrusion into protected communications. A sanctions motion itself is subject to Rule 11, while reasonable motion-related expenses may be awarded to either prevailing side.
qs: Rule 11 motions should not be made or threatened for minor, inconsequential violations of the standards prescribed by subdivision (b).
They should not be employed as a discovery device or to test the legal sufficiency or efficacy of allegations in the pleadings; other motions are available for those purposes.
As under former Rule 11, the filing of a motion for sanctions is itself subject to the requirements of the rule and can lead to sanctions.

kp.k: Discovery and other sanctioning authorities remain distinct
kp.d: Rule 11(d) excludes discovery disclosures, requests, responses, objections, and motions governed by Rules 26–37; the 1993 Notes identify Rules 26(g) and 37 as the specialized certification and sanctions framework. Rule 11 also does not displace statutory fee awards, contempt, inherent judicial powers, other rules, or 28 U.S.C. §1927.
qs: Rules 26(g) and 37 establish certification standards and sanctions that apply to discovery disclosures, requests, responses, objections, and motions.
It is appropriate that Rules 26 through 37, which are specially designed for the discovery process, govern such documents and conduct rather than the more general provisions of Rule 11.

It does not inhibit the court in punishing for contempt, in exercising its inherent powers, or in imposing sanctions, awarding expenses, or directing remedial action authorized under other rules or under 28 U.S.C. §1927.

kp.k: Amendment history distinguishes substantive revision from stylistic restyling
kp.d: The 1983 Notes describe efforts to strengthen enforcement in response to perceived ineffective deterrence and confusion. The 1993 Notes describe a corrective revision expanding obligations while constraining sanctions; their expectation of fewer sanctions motions is a stated policy prediction, not a reported outcome. The 2007 Notes characterize the amendments as stylistic only. Historical references to mandatory sanctions and discovery-motion coverage in the 1983 Notes therefore describe that earlier version, not the reproduced rule.
qs: Experience shows that in practice Rule 11 has not been effective in deterring abuses.
This revision is intended to remedy problems that have arisen in the interpretation and application of the 1983 revision of the rule.
The revision broadens the scope of this obligation, but places greater constraints on the imposition of sanctions and should reduce the number of motions for sanctions presented to the court.
These changes are intended to be stylistic only.

pts.k: The source makes no claims or predictions about AI.
pts.d: The document supplies Rule 11 and historical Advisory Committee Notes concerning litigation certifications, reasonable inquiry, and sanctions. It does not discuss AI or claim that AI changes legal services. Applying its requirements to AI-generated filings would be an analyst inference, not a claim made by this source.

pts.k: No evidence is offered for AI-related claims.
pts.d: The rule and notes cite legal authorities, litigation experience, and empirical examinations of Rule 11 sanctions. These support discussion of the procedural rule and its revisions, not findings about AI use, performance, or effects.

pts.k: No AI-related timeframe or conditions are stated.
pts.d: The amendment dates and procedural deadlines concern Rule 11, not AI adoption or its anticipated consequences. The 2007 notes describe stylistic amendments; the supplied capture date does not establish an AI-related claim.

pts.k: No group is identified as affected by AI.
pts.d: Attorneys, law firms, represented and unrepresented parties, and courts are addressed as participants subject to or administering Rule 11. The source does not distinguish AI users or describe AI-driven changes to their responsibilities, services, employment, or markets.
